Bird # 1--this appears to be either a Black-capped or a hybrid. Cold weather has arrived, and we seemed to have had some movement in our chickadee population. The hybrid zone of Black-capped and Carolina Chickadees lies a few miles north at the moment, so our breeders are Carolina. Some winters, we see flocks of Black-capped irrupting from the north. We also may see movement of hybrids below their breeding grounds.

I spotted this adorable Cedar Waxwing while on a morning dog-walking excursion outside an apartment complex in the New North End of Burlington, Vermont. This individual was seen popping in and out of tall juniper shrubs planted in the courtyard of the apartments, and moving up to the small saplings around the building as well. I didn’t see this individual fly very far, for it just popped up and down these small distances, calling to another nearby and then descending into the upper parts of the shrubs. Although I didn’t see it fly far, it flew very quickly for such a little bird and was quite difficult to capture from a far distance, for I couldn’t get extremely close since it was very wary of me and the little French bulldog that I walk (hence the awful quality and distant image). 
	Although quick, I was definitely able to observe the cedar waxwings wing shape each time it took flight. While I believe it is classified as an elliptical wing shape, I thought it looked quite different from a nearby Black-capped Chickadee flying around that also has elliptical wings; the Cedar Waxwing had slightly more elongated and pointed wings while the Chickadee’s seemed rounder. I watched it move up and down these little trees and flap its wings faster than I could blink. The movements were short and sharp, yet efficient and purposeful. 
When I think of the birds I see on almost a daily basis at my home and my place of work in Charlotte (i.e. American Crow, House Sparrow, Red-tailed Hawk), none of them have wings that are anything like the Cedar Waxwing. While the American Crow and House Sparrow both also have elliptical wings, which are good for flying short distances in crowded areas (i.e. Burlington or a nearby forest), they are both much shorter and rounder. Red-tailed Hawks have passive-soaring wings, which allows for them to circle and hover above large landscapes, which makes sense given that I see Red-tailed hawks very often at the very open farm I work at in Charlotte. 
While we couldn’t get too close to each other, I was very excited to meet this Cedar Waxwing. I have a special place in my heart for any little songbird with a crest, for the Tufted Titmouse and Northern Cardinal were always among my favorite backyard birds as a kid. I feel honored that I was able to hang out with it and watch it bounce around this rather urban and busy part of Burlington, even if it was just for a couple minutes.

The black-capped chickadee (Poecile atricapillus) is a small, nonmigratory, North American passerine bird that lives in deciduous and mixed forests. It is a member of the Paridae family, also known as tits. It has a distinct black cap on its head, a black bib underneath, and white cheeks. It has a white belly, buff sides, and grey wings, back, and tail. The bird is well known for its vocalizations, including its fee-bee song and its chick-a-dee-dee-dee call, from which it derives its name.
